review: Peak game!
Cryptark is a twin stick-style rogue-like that blends frenetic action with careful planning to create something really special.

CRYPTARK, developed and published by Alientrap, is a roguelike twin-stick shooter that distinguishes itself by blending intense real-time combat with a layer of strategic planning that feels closer to a tactical operation than a straightforward action game. Set in a grim, industrial sci-fi universe, it places players in the role of a hired mercenary sent to infiltrate derelict alien warships, dismantle their defenses, and destroy their cores for profit. While the premise sounds simple, the execution is far more nuanced, transforming each mission into a careful balance between preparation, precision, and resource management.

What immediately sets CRYPTARK apart is how much emphasis it places on pre-mission planning. Before entering a ship, players must assemble a loadout using a limited budget, choosing from a variety of weapons, tools, and support items. This system introduces a constant economic tension, as every piece of equipment has a cost and every action during a mission consumes resources. Ammunition, repairs, and utility items all draw from the same pool, meaning that reckless play can quickly lead to financial collapse. This structure forces players to think beyond raw firepower, encouraging efficient, calculated approaches rather than brute-force tactics.

Once inside a ship, the game shifts into fast-paced twin-stick shooting, but even here, strategy remains central. Each vessel is composed of interconnected systems—shield generators, repair nodes, enemy production units—that directly influence the difficulty of the encounter. Rather than simply clearing enemies, players must decide which systems to disable first, often navigating dangerous layouts while under constant pressure. The result is a layered gameplay experience where movement, targeting, and decision-making all intersect. Success depends not just on reflexes, but on understanding how to dismantle the ship’s infrastructure in the most efficient way possible.

Procedural generation plays a significant role in maintaining variety. Each ship features a different layout, enemy composition, and system arrangement, ensuring that no two missions unfold in exactly the same way. This unpredictability keeps the gameplay fresh and encourages adaptability, as players cannot rely on memorization alone. However, it also introduces moments where difficulty can feel uneven, particularly when challenging layouts are paired with limited resources. This tension between randomness and fairness is a defining part of the experience, rewarding players who can adjust their strategies on the fly.

The game’s progression system is intentionally restrained. While players can unlock new equipment and options by completing missions and collecting resources, each run largely stands on its own. There is no heavy reliance on permanent upgrades to carry players forward; instead, improvement comes from mastering the game’s systems and making smarter decisions. This design reinforces the game’s focus on skill and knowledge, but it can also make early failures feel punishing, especially when progress is lost due to a single costly mistake.

Visually, CRYPTARK embraces a dense, mechanical aesthetic that complements its tone. The interiors of alien ships are filled with industrial details, flickering lights, and destructive effects that give each mission a sense of urgency. Combat is visually chaotic but remains readable, with explosions and weapon effects adding impact without overwhelming the player. The audio design enhances this atmosphere, combining mechanical sounds and a tense soundtrack to create a constant sense of pressure as players navigate hostile environments.

One of the game’s most notable strengths is how it merges two seemingly different gameplay styles into a cohesive whole. The deliberate pacing of planning and system management contrasts sharply with the frantic nature of combat, yet the two elements support each other effectively. This duality gives CRYPTARK a unique identity, setting it apart from more traditional roguelike shooters. However, it also contributes to its difficulty, as players must be comfortable juggling both strategic thinking and real-time execution.

The challenge level is undeniably high, and it may not appeal to everyone. Mistakes can be costly, and the combination of limited resources and procedural unpredictability means that failure is often part of the learning process. For some players, this creates a rewarding sense of tension and accomplishment, while for others, it may feel overly punishing. The game demands patience and a willingness to engage deeply with its systems, offering little in the way of shortcuts or safety nets.

In the end, CRYPTARK is a tightly designed experience that succeeds by committing fully to its core ideas. It offers a compelling blend of strategy and action, wrapped in a distinctive sci-fi setting that reinforces its themes of risk and survival. While its demanding nature and economic constraints may limit its accessibility, those who embrace its systems will find a deeply satisfying and highly replayable game that rewards careful planning and precise execution.

Cryptark is a great game at its core, but it needs a touch more heart and charm. A lot of the enemies, boss 'modules' and procedurally generated dungeons were designed with more detail than the player's own avatar, weapons and abilities. 

The gist of this game is...

- Start a new campaign in a save slot.
- Choose a robotic exoskeleton.
- Move through multiple 'phases' of your campaign, each phase you are clearing a salvage-ship dungeon buy defeating its 'brain core' (the salvage-ships have autonomous AI systems).
- You get a choice of four salvage-ship dungeons to excavate in each phase. Once you choose the ship you want to tackle, there's a pre-planning phase where you can test out weapons, add / remove weapons and generally plan out your salvage mission with a map using a singular waypoint.
- Salvage ships have multiple supportive systems that will shield, spawn enemies, control stationary turrets around the ship, etc.
- At the end of these phases you get to the endphase, the 'Cryptark'. This a really big salvage-ship with every support system inside of it (it's a real challenge to destroy and navigate the Cryptark and tests your knowledge of the game).

Final thing to note is that as you clear salvage-ships you get money. There are bonus tasks for each salvage ship which grant you more money. You use that money to upgrade your exoskeleton with weapons and ammo. (The exoskeletons are called 'Gunheads' in-game but I prefer to think of them as 'exoskeletons' as it's a little easier to visualise if you haven't played the game). You find new weapons as randomised interactable objects inside each salvage ship; usually a ship has two-five scattered around. 

There's also rogue mode which operates the same way, but your health, weapons and ammo carry over through each phase. Now that's all swell and fine...the game functions great...very little glitches...the art design is superbly original...the soundtrack is good....but there's something missing: a real loadout system.

Once you've put in about 20-30 hours in the game's repeating campaign mode, you should be able to simply create your own robotic exoskeleton however you like. Instead what you get are 7-8 preset, unlockable exoskeletons. Each has a unique ability that is essential to master if you're going to advance through the campaign. The default exoskeleton has a dash, which is useful for getting time bonuses, but other abilities like the shield built into the 'Rook' exoskeleton or the teleport function of the stealth-based exoskeleton are much, much more powerful. Once you've unlocked all these goodies, it becomes a bit trite not being able to mix and match unique abilities to different frames. One unique ability, one frame (with the appropriate set of starting weapons / gear) shouldn't be that hard to implement and balance. Artificial difficulty and scarcity have their limits even in roguelikes...

Another minor gripe is that almost every smaller enemy you shoot at in the salvage ship-dungeons feels over-tuned in comparison to the weapons you're given to kill those enemies. The challenge becomes deciding which 'hard counter' weapons you want to take into a dungeon just to avoid certain enemy types.

The flow of the game often becomes very predictable after you've spent a lot of time unlocking exoskeletons and learning the different weapons available. You're free to choose which boss 'modules' or 'systems' to destroy while in these dungeons, but it is ALWAYS more prudent to destroy 1-3 specific modules first (Shuffle, Failsafe and Repair) then go after the rest. The ships are procedurally generated, but you are always tackling them with a predictable mission plan. Once you understand the high priority modules to destroy, you'll always get to the Cryptark with a lot of cash to spare, which is nice, but sort-of defeats the purpose of procedurally-generated dungeons with randomised rewards.

One also finds this predictability in the game's main challenge: collecting 'alien artifacts'. These are unique items that essentially carry over to each run, enabling you to unlock new exoskeletons as I mentioned earlier. Artifacts are gained by completing a dungeon under a specific, really tough condition. One of them for instance is "Don't use [Shielding Items]". You'll quickly find that certain exoskeletons you unlock excel at completing these conditions better than others. For instance the second exoskeleton you unlock, called 'Rook', has a shield built in, thus you don't need to buy a Shielding Item in the pre-planning phase and you essentially circumvent the challenge all-together. This is the most obvious example, but I hope the point is made with regards to predictability: the player's creativity isn't tested by these challenges, they all seem to have very limited solutions. Not only that, I've seen people on web forums rightfully criticise this type of 'limited challenge' design...and this really hammers home my original point:


[b]Why design all these gameplay elements (cool weapons, cool ships, cool abilities) and then disincentivise the player from truly using those elements to their full potential?[/b]


As a personal aside, I find that the newfound obsession with speed-running family-oriented platformers like Mario and the strange cultural discourse around indie-shoot-'em-ups from Japan within the animé community has a regressive impact on a lot of developpers and 'gamers'. It is fans who dump the entire code of Super Mario 64 or who play dozens and dozens of vaporware 'Doujin' shoot-em-ups who end up having a very rigid understanding of video-game history and game design. These fans not only re-interpret older games into their cultural rigidity, but they go into video-game design with no understanding of how to create emergent gameplay or tailor their games to a wide variety of playstyles.

That's just an aside, however, I don't fully believe that Cryptark approaches that Rigidity of Design, if you will, but there's enough sadistic challenges and over-tuned design elements that bring it very close. Obviously the game is very enjoyable, but to 'enjoy' something is meaningless in the context of a review. 

I'd much rather describe a 'lack' or a 'function' within a review instead of describing 'traits' or a 'cultural satisfaction'; the former two are useful and memorable, the latter two are effete and personal. 

Bottom line: Cryptark is a roguelike with a distinct lack of emergent gameplay and it has Metroidvania-esque exploration without the ability to sequence break; despite my personal time enjoying the game, Cryptark could have implemented a gentler touch towards its own mission challenges, exoskeleton avatars and combat design.

Seriously an underappreciated gem.  I know that Gunhead got a little more fanfare, and that it was the FPS remake of this game, but if you ask me, I just find CRYPTARK more engaging. The music rocks, the sound design is crisp, and the voice acting is superb, and the writing it's over is fun for what's here. The controls are responsive, the gunplay and planning is incredibly fun, pausing mid mission on the map to reasses and plot routes without losing time is an amazing choice by the devs, and the arsenal is expansive. The alternative suits are meaningfully different to use and the lore bits from acquired Artifacts add to the worldbuilding immensely. It also doesn't waste time with a long overarching plot right out of the gate, and the tutorial is equally succinct and competent. 

You're a privateering crew, you're hired to scuttle some alien wetware shipwrecks. The big haul is the CRYPTARK. If you fail, you're fired, The frogman voiced by Jerma, surprisingly, does a fairly awesome job of getting to the point of the controls before you're taught how to use the map and read the modules. Every module has it's own challenge to subvert to destroy it, and they interact meaningfully with each other to force you to plan a route. The more money you make, the more money you can afford to use on big guns, or afford to lose if you crash and burn on a mission. There's a Campaign mode which is this, and a Rogue game mode where you go out off the books to scuttle a separate flotilla of wrecks for your crews own profit, complete with it's own artifacts. 

It wastes no time getting to the fun stuff, the fun stuff is actually fun, and you can stop between missions which are usually only 8-12 minutes long, assuming you even use all that time and don't speedrun for the extra cash. 

I genuinely cannot fathom why more people don't know about this game, or why it hasn't gotten the appreciation it deserves. I genuinely feel awful redeeming this game for free way back when. Please, support the devs. Purchase Gunhead if you're more into FPS games, I'd say it's a lot like if CRYPTARK met Tower of Guns. I prefer being able to choose the stuff you get licenses for before rushing into the fray, but they are different enough games, and I would definitely suggest you at least try Cryptark. The amount of people that have this game and haven't even played it genuinely upsets me.

Cryptark takes a different approach to the whole "loadout cost" system that most other games utilize, where your cost of everything is tallied by how much of the stuff you've used. Cryptark instead charges you a flat value at the beginning of your runs into the derelict ships of the Alien Flotilla, and so you better use it or lose it. I've found this system to be very refreshing, as it makes sense for a corporation to charge you for all of the equipment you're taking into a run with you, though the fact you don't really get money back for unspent equipment is a little weird.

Enemy variety is interesting, but the enemy variety in the game swings wildly between enemies that are extremely powerful and obnoxious to deal with, to enemies that basically do nothing to you except shoot weird purple goo at you. Leviathan's and Juggernaut's are good examples of this, as they're both meant to be big and bad enemies, but Leviathan's never once caused me problems, whereas Juggernauts were a constant pain.

Cryptark as a game is a little bit short. I've played every single bit of content there is in under 10 hours, and unlocked every specific frame for use in the Rogue and Cryptark Excavation modes. One of the biggest complaints I've got for the game is the lack of frame variety whilst you're in the campaign, as there are obviously more available due to their appearance in the Rogue and Excavation modes, so having them in the story as optional upgrades which you find aboard some ships would add some much needed spice to the game.

Cryptark's arsenal is varied but not particularly super interesting unless you're lucky enough to find a BUNCH of licenses for weird and cool weapons during your campaign run. Along with that, many of the weapons are just genuinely outclassed by others within the games available arsenal, making for a situation where you'll be asking yourself "Why would I bother using this weapon, when I could just continue using THIS one?", because even if you try to play stealthily later on the game becomes more frantic with requiring you to kill more and more things.

[b]Overall[/b], I'd give Cryptark an 8/10, and would suggest you pick it up if it's on sale.

The funny thing is I dont actually want to give this a thumbs down, but I also don't want to give this a thumbs up either. I guess I am leaning more towards thumbs down, Sure would be nice if there were more options thn up or down but there ya go. 

The game overall is fun but frustrating, theres a lot I want to say about this game but I dnt want to leave a wall of text so I will focus on the frustrating over the fun because its a thumbs down review not thumbs up. There are probably 3X that which will tell you whats good about the game. Here we go. 

The game modes. There are two game modes, rogue and campaign. Both have a strange diffuclty curve you got to learn to process before jumping into a new mission. Rogue starts you off with a pretty decent difficulty and not too friendly for new players, it also doesn't refill any health of ammunition between missions. There are items you can find to refill both of these but they are a bit scarce, leaving rogue to be something for the veterans who get tired of campaign and are used to the resource grind. 

The only other mode is campaign, which leaves a lot to be desired. It plays more as a glorified tutorial thn anything. You go from one selection of derelict ships and choose on to board. You are given a selection of Icons to let you know whats on board, but you are not told what said Icons actually mean so its a guess to whats on the ship until you memorize them over time. Once you start a mission the difficulty curve is actually REALLY drastic. I think this is due to the campaign being generally short, you can beat it in under 2 hours. It suppose to have a replay value by unlocking new mech like outfits to try, but besides that it feels rather lacking in replay department. 

It also did something that I wish less rogue likes would do. That is, having a less than instant restart. It's a rogue like, you are suppose to die and go back at it but so many of these games dont have that restart that lets you start a fresh life and dive into the action right away. When you know you got a bad run you just want to press ESC and RETRY, Nope, not here either. In fact in campaign you are significantly punished for dying. In a game genre built around, try, try, try again this game rips away a large sum of your funds you are given as earnings upon every death leaving a real bad taste in your mouth.

In the end what ultimately leaned my rating towards thumbs down was, each game session lasted barley an hour, and I didnt even really want to return. But I spent cash on the game so In a way I felt like I gotta. The game is heavily lacking in a lot of features that should give it depth, but it's just an average shoot'em up rogue like. The kind we get five dozen of every year. It doesn't do enough to stick out from the bunch, and it doesn't have that much replay value in comparison to the competition.

The initial difficulty in cryptark resides in identifying the different ship systems and in which order to destroy them.
After that it's just a matter of navigating a huge labyrinthine spaceship and destroying it piece by piece within the alloted time. Despite the monotonous and repetitive aspect, I could see this being a comfy roguelite. 
Unfortunately the game is spoiled by bad playability.

First the enemies zip around way too fast, seemingly unmarred by the laws of physic. And your projectiles are too slow to aim at them, so you can only aim in their general direction and hope they'll run into your bullets. Which is a problem when the bullets are limited.
And your own mech is often turned into a air hockey puck by the constant explosions and collisions that push you around.

Second problem is the bad visibility, in great part due to the 3D rendering baking everything into colored normal mapped lighting, and the fact everything is of the same hue. It's very difficult to tell what's a wall and what's not and most of the traps are hard to see until they start damaging you.
These two problems are compounded by the fact that the camera is moved toward your crosshair, thus greatly diminishing your environmental awareness, especially when you're in a tight spot.
Most of your deaths will be unfair deaths caused by an enemy hitting you from behind after you've been bounced around and trapped between walls and a damage zone.

The equipment you can pick up during the run is rather scarce and most of it worthless.

The ridiculous inflationary economics don't make sense and are just there to force some fake scarcity onto the run, and will provide you with even more unfair deaths. For example it happened a couple times that the game ended my run due to low money, even though I just beat the level.

In the last level (out of 5), it's very likely that he map will generate two repair systems (repairing each other) with an assortment of shuffling/failsafe/jammer systems, which means it's very unlikely you'll be able to beat it.

Cryptark gets what it means to be a roguelike, at least for the campaign mode.

Everything is a calculated risk and investment of your main resource, money: for example, before committing to a mission you choose what weapons to bring with you, for each weapon you pay more the more ammo you bring, and you do NOT get anything back for unspent ammo.
Same for consumable items, such as repair packs and nuclear demolition charges.
Ammo-less weapons, such as melee and energy options? Those have a price too, and they might turn out to be far more expensive than conventional counterparts if you don't get enough use out of them.
Passive upgrades? You guessed it, you have to pay for each mission you want to bring them with you, also they take up an item slot each: sure, immunity to environmental hazards is nice, but is it really worth it over higher damage (and thus more bang for you buck)?
More mech suit armor, aka more starting hitpoints? Pay up.
You find a repair pod on a mission? You need money to use it.
Even dying is just a steep repair bill, and as long as you can afford it you're free to try again.
And if you want to earn more money, you have no option but to pick harder missions and complete more bonus objectives.

The mission themselves can get pretty brutal, which I also like: defense turrets on the outside of the ship that basically guarantee damage if you try to cross their firing range, factory systems creating drones indefinitely and at a concerning pace, repair systems steadily undoing your progress, shuffle systems invalidating long term plans, nuclear systems being nuclear systems...
Of course, if you manage to keep the costs low in the early missions you can bring out bigger and badder guns for the later and harder ones, and maybe even afford a couple deaths.

Only two things persist between mission in a campaign: your money, and the tech you discover on ships (which unlocks weapons and items for you to use).
As a result, the success of a run depends almost exclusively on your skill, both in the mission itself and in the planning before it: there's no getting carried by a couple lucky finds as in so many roguelites, you need to get good and consistently make smart choices the whole way through.

The rogue mode is, oddly enough, much more relaxed: no buying anything, just equipping what you find in missions and replacing it once it runs dry, and what you can find is far more plentiful than what you can afford to bring in campaign mode.

On the negative side, the game is full of technical issues, mostly hard crashes: thankfully the missions are not too long (usually 15-30 minutes for the late game ones) and the game USUALLY allows you to reload back to the start without losing anything.
Sometime you can also see badly generated missions, for example unreachable core/shield systems making things unwinnable, but that's pretty rare in my experience.

This is a good ass game. You can complete it in an hour or two, sure, but it is worth the price.

You play as a guy in a mech suit scrapping large ships for sale later. These ship all have their defenses activated of course. 
Almost no single idea in this game is bad, its when combined it becomes obvious the developers just decided it was good enough and sent it out.  
You collect many different and unique weapons throughout the game, but none of them are cost effective when combined with the number of enemies you'll be facing endgame. The weapons that are cost effective for what they are don't hit hard enough and the ones that do are far too expensive. I think the game intends you to balance that out, but there is no balance. It simply does not work out. You always need more. Health, ammo, weapons. 
When exploring the ships the most dreaded enemy for me personally is the most basic melee only stabby boys. They're way too difficult to hit, depending on the ship they're literally endless and can teleport, and have a lingering hit box that you'll likely run into after they're done attacking. Picking up specific weapons to deal with them is an option, but those same weapons aren't useful anywhere else. Your basic melee as useless against moving targets as it flings you around violently. 
The giant heavy armored guys are just a slight nuisance in comparison. All enemies can move through walls and doors, even attack through them. You cant of course. Which adds to the absurd difficulty in dealing with many enemies at once. 
In prepping these ships for sale. you have to take out certain systems in order to get to the brain. Again, fine at the start of the game. Repair systems are the worst. Ships can have two more then a minute apart in a straight journey, effectively making finishing the ship off impossible, as it only take a minute to fully repair a system. Example. To kill the core you need to destroy two repair systems, and bare minimum two shield generators. And do it within one minute. That's already very difficult without being hounded by hoards of bots. Ideally you want to take out the repair systems and deal with the rest, but it literally doesn't matter when you can barely make it to the other repair system even if you make a B Line for it. This is also compounded by the fact that you may not have a map to work it as the ship might have a cloak system, which also needs breaking. 
There's a mechanic in the game where to open certain doors you need to use the directional keys, requiring you to take your hand away from the mouse, which is how you aim and shoot. A fine and interesting idea on its own, but when combined with the fact that 60% of the time it glitches and doesn't work forcing you to do it again, certain enemies can lock you in place and force you to do this. Which might not be so bad except for, again the sheer amount of bots later on in addition with how you've handled your loadout. You may not even be equipped to be in a massive cqb. In which case you're just screwed. 
There's also the matter of bots just not being hit by you randomly. The bullet (or whatever) goes right through them and nothing. The game likes to crash pretty often as well. 
This game is comprised of many pretty moving parts that just don't go well together. It needs adjustment. I've seen people compare this to FTL, but FTL is an infinitely more balanced game where the difficulty makes sense. 

The thing that could be done to make me change my mind is an overall readjustment of enemy number or re-balancing of equipment cost. Everything else I can let go, but I feel these two particular aspects ruin the fun. It's just not fun to play.

[h2]Review after 15 Hours: A Unique Roguelike Sci-Fi Shooter[/h2]

Cryptark delivers a challenging and engaging experience that combines tactical planning with fast-paced action. With its procedural generation, unique suit abilities, and satisfying combat mechanics, it stands out as a rewarding roguelike shooter.

[h3]Pros:[/h3]
[list]
[*] [b]Replayability:[/b] Procedural generation ensures that derelict ships have unique layouts each time, making every run feel fresh. The variety of suits also adds depth to gameplay, encouraging experimentation with different strategies. 
[*] [b]Atmosphere & Soundtrack:[/b] Excellent lighting effects and immersive music create a gritty sci-fi ambiance that pulls you into the game’s world.
[*] [b]Satisfying Combat:[/b] Shooting mechanics feel impactful, with a wide range of weapons and tools to customize your playstyle. 
[*] [b]Intruder Suit Gameplay:[/b] The Intruder suit brings a methodical, stealthy approach to missions, offering a refreshing change of pace and making strategic planning essential. 
[*] [b]Challenge:[/b] Missions require careful resource management and strategic targeting of ship systems, rewarding players who plan ahead.
[/list]
[h3]Cons:[/h3] 
[list]
[*] [b]Steep Learning Curve:[/b] The game can feel overwhelming at first, especially with multiple systems, weapons, and loadout options to master. 
[*] [b]Difficulty Spikes:[/b] The mid-game (around derelict ship 3) introduces a significant jump in challenge, and the final ship, Cryptark, is on a completely different difficulty level. 
[*] [b]UI Controls:[/b] The UI interface in the menus of the game feels clunky at times. Better mouse integration could improve the overall flow. 
[/list]

[h3]Final Thoughts:[/h3] Cryptark is a must-play for fans of challenging roguelike shooters with a strategic edge. Its procedural generation and variety of suits keep gameplay fresh and replayable, while its combat and atmosphere are top-notch. However, players should prepare for a steep learning curve and some punishing difficulty spikes.

Rating: 3.5/5
If you enjoy tactical gameplay, tough challenges, and a gritty sci-fi aesthetic, Cryptark is well worth diving into.

Attention, [u] ce jeu n'est pas en shoot'em up [/u] mais plutôt un roguelike stratégique.

C'est écrit en toute lettre dans la description du produit, mais ça va mieux en le répétant.

En effet, lors des premières parties, il est tentant, voir naturel, d'utiliser les différentes armes à disposition (grenades, mitrailleuses, lasers, etc.) et de "foncer dans le tas" en tirant sur tout ce qui bouge.

En tombant dans ce travers, on finit par se casser les dents sur les défenses des vaisseaux de niveau élevé, en particulier sur le Hulk final de la campagne (le fameux "Cryptark"). En réalité, en faisant cela, on passe complètement à côté du jeu.

Donc, méfiance par rapport aux évaluations (qui peuvent être de bonne foi) critiquant la courbe de difficulté qui augmenterait trop vite.

[b] Tout l'intérêt de Cryptark réside dans la planification de nos actions [/b], ce qui est possible principalement grâce à la carte ainsi qu'avec la possibilité de mettre le jeu en pause à tout moment (particulièrement utile en fin de campagne et absolument VITAL dans le mode "Rogue")

Planifier, planifier et encore planifier, c'est ça le secret. Une fois cela compris, ce jeu est [b] un vrai bonheur ! [/b]

Ainsi, il est particulièrement jouissif et gratifiant de venir à bout d'un énorme vaisseau parce qu'on a réussit à démanteler ses différents systèmes défensifs de façon logique, rapide et impitoyable.


Au sujet de l'aspect stratégique, j'ai remarqué une seule petite faiblesse dans le jeu : 
Sur la carte on peut (et c'est plus qu'utile !) pointer tel ou tel objectif, comme un système à attaquer ou un équipement à ramasser. Dans ce cas, un itinéraire est d'office proposé, ce qui permet de suivre une voie qui s'affiche en pointillé.

En théorie, cela permet de se déplacer d'une zone à une autre sans avoir besoin de se référer sans cesse à la carte. Mais malheureusement, le pathfinding est complètement foireux et il n'est pas rare que le jeu nous incite à passer par des itinéraires invraisemblables, sources de danger et de perte de temps.
A noter que les itinéraires les plus courts ne sont pas toujours les meilleurs, à cause notamment des déplacements beaucoup plus rapides dans le vide spatial (attention quand même aux éventuels canons antiaériens).

Donc, afin de palier ce léger raté, il faut faire pause dès que nécessaire et de manière répétitive s'il le faut. Cela casse un peu le rythme du jeu mais, à mon sens, ça reste tout à fait supportable.


S'agissant de l'aspect action, la variété des armes disponibles est très appréciable. Chaque équipement à ses points faibles, points forts et spécificités éventuelles : cadence de tir, portée, puissance, effet de recul, fonctions spéciales (têtes chercheuses, effet de zone, tirs à travers les murs, déclenchement à distance et j'en passe ...)
Bref, en fonction de son style de jeu, chaque joueur aura possibilité de trouver ses armes favorites et combinaisons préférées. 

A ce propos, je conseille de bien se roder sur le mode Campaign avant d'attaquer le mode Rogue.
En effet, la campagne offre la possibilité de changer d'arme et de refaire le plein de munitions entre chaque mission, ce qui permet de se familiariser avec chaque équipement et de tester différentes combinaisons.
En Rogue, cela n'est pas possible ; on ne peut pas revenir à la base pour se soigner et se réapprovisionner en cartouches. En plus aucun dépôt de munition n'est disponible pendant les missions. Du coup, on est obligé de chercher de nouvelles d'armes régulièrement. Connaitre ces dernières est un vrai avantage (petit conseil au passage : essayez de trouver une arme à énergie correcte que vous pourrez conserver étant donné qu'elle ne tombe jamais à court de munition) 


Quelques mots rapides sur l'aspect technique :

Avec une manette correcte, la maniabilité est très agréable et instinctives.
Par "manette correcte", j'entends une manette classique avec 2 sticks, 4 boutons directionnels, 4 boutons de tranches, ...

Sans être mirobolants, les graphismes, sons et musiques sont satisfaisant et ont le mérite de donner une vraie personnalité au jeu.
L'univers visuel, à base d'environnements essentiellement industriels et de créatures cybernétiques étranges, est plutôt sombre, froid et effrayant. Les musiques de type electro sont dans le ton. Les bruitages sont efficaces et reconnaissables.


Pour finir, la durée de vie est comme tout le reste : très satisfaisante.

Les modes Campaign et Rogue offrent de quoi faire, surtout si on veut tester les différents types d'armes et de personnages (mention spéciale à l'exosquelette Intruder qui permet de jouer en mode infiltration grâce au mode de furtivité pré-équipé). 

Le mode Cryptark Excavation (que l'on débloque en finissant Campaign + Rogue) offre peu de durée de vie supplémentaire. Ceci dit, il a tout son intérêt.
Je n'en dit pas plus pour ne pas spoiller.

Je ne l'ai pas testé, mais je précise qu'un mode coopératif à deux sur le même écran est également présent (encore un bon point).

A really good action roguelike. You're a mech pilot who infiltrates derelict spaceships to blow up the central core controlling the ship's automated defenses. 

Aside from the core, every level is filled with a random assortment of defenses. There's attack drones, plus ship facilities that do distressing things if you leave them un-blown-up for too long: creating an endless stream of drones, controlling turret guns throughout the level, repairing destroyed ship systems, etc. But you can freely pause the game to study a radar scan of the stage layout and enemy positions and there are also lots of airlocks scattered around that let you escape and re-enter the ship from different points. 

So basically the game uses the random generation of a roguelike really well- level generation consistently creates interesting problems for you to deal with, and the game gives you freedom of movement around a stage and the ability to carefully plan out your next move, letting you pull off freeform solutions and decide which targets to prioritize. Sometimes you can sneak into the ship for a scalpel strike on some target and zip back out before the airlock even has time to close on you; sometimes the best option is a gunfight with a posse of drones. The time pressure from ship systems, plus the cost of ammo (yeah, you have a budget) pushes you to plan your moves carefully. But if you play well you'll be swimming in cash to buy goodies- mainly ammo for the neat pile of random guns you build up over a run.

The selection of mechs is cool. They've all got interesting special abilities- one can enter bullet time, another can both tele-hop past walls and snipe through them, letting it mess with maps something awful. A couple mechs simply have the ability to dash, which turns out to actually be quite versatile and fun to use... and there's a few others, it's a nice variety pack.

I bought this game way back when it came out and have never beaten it. I decided to give it another try and am reminded how great it is. I wanted to make a review for it so hopefully other people can understand how great it is as well.

So this game is incredible and very unique! It is a combination roguelike sidescroller twin stick shooter (which to be fair isn't as unique of a genre now as it was back when this came out) but what does make it stand out is the absolutely amazing theme and visuals. I love sci-fi horror, and the enemies in this game are an absolute treat to destroy. 

The gameplay loop is that you are presented with a choice of ~5 ships to salvage (different ship types exist that have different characteristics). You pick a ship to tackle, pick your mech's loadout (more on that later), then enter the ship and destroy various modules within it while being attacked by creepy alien robot zombies. Along the way you can pick up health or ammo refills (although you probably won't, again more on that later) as well as technology stations which give you more options to equip your mech for the next mission. The modules do stuff to make your job harder, from as basic as "makes another module invulnerable while this one is alive" to "causes a massive nuclear explosion whenever you destroy another module" and many more brands of horribleness. Each of these modules is more than capable of defending itself and is a little mini-boss fight. The final goal is to destroy the central control module which ends the level. Then you get a new selection of harder ships. If you fail you either end the run on roguelike mode or on campaign mode get kicked out into a new selection of same difficulty ships (which is almost as bad, yet again see later). 

You are on a clock while you do all this by the way (more on that later), so pick a couple systems that you most need to destroy and find an efficient route through the ship to get to the main control. At least you can see the whole map of the ship beforehand and come up with a loadout and strategy (most of the time. A jammmer module exists and it is exactly as horrible as you think it would be).

The other unique thing about this game is also why I will never beat it in a million years. Remember how I kept saying "more on that later"? Well, it's later! Your expedition into this derelict space fleet has a certain budget, and the loadout you select before going into any given level costs money. Want more starting health? Costs money. Want to swap out for that awesome rocket launcher you just found? Costs money. Want to bring more ammo for your weapons since you were close to running out last time? Costs money. Want to bring a repair kit or other cool gadget? Costs money. Go over the time limit for the level? You guessed it, costs money.

Fortunately your initial budget is not all you ever get to complete the game. Every ship that you select to salvage has a certain base reward for completion, along with challenges that you can complete for a bonus reward. These can be quite substantial if you complete all of them, equaling or exceeding the base payout, but be warned some of them are absolutely miserable to complete. A very common challenge is "no resupply pods" so you know those nice health and ammo refill stations scattered around the ship I mentioned earlier? Yeah, you won't be using those.

It does make the game a very weird choose your own adventure difficulty which I love but freely admit I still haven't mastered. If you want to max out on ammo and really strong weapons, strap as much armor on your mech as you can, and bring tons of cool gadgets you totally can, and the mission will most likely be super easy. You will also most likely not break even on that mission and have less money for your next one which will be harder. I tend to be the opposite and try way too hard to horde money at the expense of loadout while also going for challenges, which inevitably gets me blown up (and kicked over to another set of ships with no reward). 

Anyway, I highly recommend people play this game. It's been around for a while but I still think it holds up well enough to buy today.

I feel like I'm constantly fighting the game, when it comes to trying new strategies and equipment.  Layered throughout missions are tech terminals that provide the player with new equipment to use in future levels.  It is encouraged to get as many as possible to make your suit more versatile and open up more play styles.  The problem with this is the equipment the player unlocks is usually very expensive.  I'm hesitant to modify the suit, as the money earned at the end of missions is barely a net positive, after factoring in the equipment costs of the suit; and equipping more expensive gear only makes the issue worse.  In missions, there are three side goals the player can accomplish to earn extra money, however the missions also have a time limit, and if that limit is reached the player will earn reduced money at the end of the mission.

The tactical decision making in the planning phase is counteracted by the constant influx of enemies, barely giving you anytime to breathe and act out your plan once your're in the ship, and this problem is made worse if the ship contains factories that constantly produce more enemies.  The planning phase and side goals incentivizes players to take their time to execute their plan, but the time limit on missions and constant spawning of enemies incenvivizes players to get through the mission as quickly as possible before the time runs out or they die, creating a confusing and frustrating gameplay experience.

Finally, the difficulty curve of the game is terrible.  The first two to three ships you infiltrate are fairly easy, while the fourth and fifth ships provide a greater challenge, but to a reasonable degree.  The final mission ruins this curve completely.  The most systems I've seen on a ship on level 5 is 13, the final level that comes right after has 22 systems.  This massive spike in difficulty leaves the player completely unprepared for the challenge that lay ahead.  Players are likely to fail the mission multiple times, and every time the player fails a mission, they lose a considerable amount of money, discouraging them from using the more expensive and powerful gear, further decreasing their chances of success on the final level.
